Review: Review Summary vs. Signed Agreement

Harbor Research / Cedar Systems — Summary dated 22 Sep 2026 checked against excerpts dated 20 Sep 2026. Three material contradictions found.

1. Liability — "All claims are capped at twelve months of fees."

Controlling passage (agreement):

§8.1: "Except as provided in Section 8.2, each party's aggregate liability is limited to the fees paid in the twelve months before the event giving rise to the claim."
§8.2: "The limit in Section 8.1 does not apply to fraud or willful misconduct."

Contradiction: The summary states the cap applies to all claims. The agreement carves out fraud and willful misconduct, which are excluded from the cap.

Practical difference: In a fraud or willful-misconduct claim, the party's exposure is not limited to 12 months of fees — full damages may be recoverable. Relying on the summary would cause the customer to mistakenly assume the fee cap still applies even to the worst conduct, and could undercut its leverage or recovery in a serious misconduct case.

2. Deletion — "All customer data must be deleted within thirty days of termination."

Controlling passage (agreement):

§11.1: "Customer data will be deleted from active systems within thirty days after termination."
§11.2: "Encrypted disaster-recovery backups may be retained for up to ninety days after termination. Access to those backups is limited to disaster recovery and legal preservation obligations."

Contradiction: The summary says all customer data must be deleted within 30 days. The agreement only requires deletion from active systems within 30 days and explicitly permits encrypted DR backups to be retained up to 90 days after termination.

Practical difference: The customer cannot assume its data is fully gone by day 30. Encrypted copies may persist on DR backups for up to 90 days. This matters for data-retention, security, and compliance expectations (e.g., the customer cannot represent or rely on "data deleted within 30 days" as complete), and it leaves a window in which the vendor still holds the data (albeit access-restricted).

3. Termination — "The customer can terminate immediately for any service interruption."

Controlling passage (agreement):

§12.1: "A material service breach permits termination only after written notice and failure to cure within thirty days. A service interruption is not automatically a material breach."

Contradiction: The summary allows immediate termination for any service interruption. The agreement (a) requires the event to be a material breach — a mere interruption does not automatically qualify — and (b) conditions termination on written notice plus a thirty-day cure period, with termination allowed only after cure fails.

Practical difference: The customer cannot terminate immediately on any interruption. At minimum the customer must (1) establish the interruption is a material breach, (2) give written notice, and (3) wait for the 30-day cure period to run without cure. A service interruption that is not a material breach gives no termination right at all. This substantially delays and conditions the termination right that the summary describes as immediate and universal.

Note on scope (liability): §8.3 cautions that no inference should be drawn about other claim categories from excerpts not supplied, so the fraud/willful-misconduct carve-out is the only exception confirmed in these excerpts — but it is enough to make the summary's "all claims" statement inaccurate.

Bottom line: Each summary statement overstates the customer's position — the liability cap is narrower than "all claims," deletion is not complete within 30 days, and the termination right is conditional (notice + cure + materiality) rather than immediate for any interruption.
